name: PT Petrosea Tbk

frontmatter.title: Petrosea — a leveraged mining contractor priced for a recovery the contracts have not yet earned
frontmatter.summary: Petrosea is the Barito group's mining-contractor and EPC vehicle, with a record order book but a balance sheet that consumes most of its operating profit. Our most-likely case uses management's disclosed US$1,134.7m revenue expectation for the coming year, has margins recovering from the mobilisation trough and net profit only turning positive after the current interest burden; the konglo lens keeps part of today's premium, so we initiate at HOLD with a target of Rp2,191.
thesis: Petrosea is a contract business, not a coal producer — mining services, EPC and EPCI revenue is earned on overburden, construction and life-of-mine contracts, so the coal deck matters through client capex and contract awards rather than through a direct selling price [S2][S4].

The order book is the strongest part of the story — unsatisfied performance obligations of US$4,439.0m at the end of FY2025, plus two new SINI-linked life-of-mine contracts signed in July 2026 worth US$431.2m and US$89.6m — but conversion is capital-hungry and the FY2025 fleet build lifted net debt to a level where interest absorbs most of EBIT [S3][S4].

The data pack's D&A is unusable for the two years the valuation leans on — the LK shows depreciation of US$90.6m in FY2025 (plus amortisation of US$14.6m), against a pack figure of a small fraction of that, so FY2024A and FY2025A are restated from the notes and EBITDA rebuilt to US$162.9m after final tax [S4].

Our base case puts FY2026E revenue at US$1,134.7m, management's disclosed 2026 revenue expectation in the performance-obligation note (the percentage growth is our derivation, not a management-stated rate), and a gross margin of 9.7%, below the FY2025 actual because new EPC and mining contracts mobilise at lower initial margins; net profit stays negative in FY2026E before the contracts mature [S3][S4].

The market is not pricing our fundamental value — at Rp2,320 the shares trade at 2.2x the probability-weighted fundamental value today of Rp1,077.5 (0.77 in log terms), against a twelve-month fundamental value of Rp1,235. The konglo lens closes 30.0% of the log premium in its base regime (Rp2,113) and keeps the remainder; probability-weighted across its three regimes it gives a target of Rp2,191, an expected total return of -5.5% [S0][S10][S11].
The reverse DCF says the price requires FY2027E revenue growth of about 21.4%, well above our 8.0%; that gap, not the coal price, is the core of the call [S0][S4].

blocks.text: **The call.** We initiate coverage of PT Petrosea Tbk at HOLD with a twelve-month target of Rp2,191 against a last price of Rp2,320, an expected total return of -5.5% including the modelled dividend stream [S0]. The target is not our fundamental value: it is the konglo lens's most-likely price, which keeps part of the premium the shares have carried through the Barito-group era and lets it compress only gradually over the next twelve months [S10][S11].

**What the company is.** Petrosea sells mining services (overburden stripping, coal production, mine development), engineering and construction, offshore EPCI and logistics support. Group revenue was US$886.5m in FY2025 and gross profit US$112.2m; the segment split is in the section above [S2][S4]. The operating record is real: coal overburden removal rose to 135.2 million BCM in FY2025 from 106.7 million BCM, and coal production rose to 19.2 million tonnes from 18.0 million tonnes [S2]. The backlog at the end of FY2025 was US$4,439.0m of unsatisfied performance obligations, and the company signed two new life-of-mine coal contracts in July 2026 with a combined value of US$431.2m plus US$89.6m [S3][S4].

**Why the equity is not the backlog.** The contracts are executed with a large owned fleet, and the FY2025 fleet build lifted capex to US$434.3m against operating cash flow of US$48.2m, so debt rose and interest now consumes most of operating profit [S4]. Our FY2026E EBIT is US$50.6m against interest expense of US$68.0m, leaving a small pre-tax loss before the contract mix improves; net profit turns positive only in FY2027E in our base case [S3][S4]. That is why the shares can trade below our target while still sitting above our fundamental value: the market is paying for a recovery that our most-likely case says is late, not absent.

**What moves the value.** Three things: the speed at which the new SINI-linked life-of-mine contracts reach steady-state overburden volume, the gross margin on the EPC book as it converts, and the refinancing cost of the enlarged debt stack. A one-point change in gross margin is worth more to the equity than a ten-dollar move in Newcastle, because the coal price reaches Petrosea through client capex and contract awards, not through its own realised price. The reverse DCF makes the point plainly: at today's price the market is discounting FY2027E revenue growth of about 21.4%, versus our 8.0% [S0][S4].

Petrosea is an Indonesian engineering, construction and mining-services company with four disclosed revenue lines: Mining, Construction and Engineering, EPCI-Offshore Oil and Gas, and Services. Group revenue was US$886.5m in FY2025 and group gross profit US$112.2m; the segment note shows Mining, Construction and Engineering, EPCI and Services, with a small at-point-in-time coal-sale line [S4]. The company operates the largest part of its business for coal miners in Kalimantan and Sumatra and for mineral producers such as PT Vale Indonesia and PT Freeport Indonesia, and it has been expanding into offshore EPCI and logistics [S2][S4].

The business model is contract-based and capital-intensive. Petrosea is paid for overburden removal, coal hauling, mine development and construction, and it owns the heavy equipment that does the work. That is why the two operating KPIs that matter are overburden volume and coal production: in FY2025 the company moved 135.2 million BCM of coal overburden and produced 19.2 million tonnes of coal from its mining-services contracts, both records, while mineral-project material movement also grew [S2]. Revenue is recognised over time for services and at a point in time for coal sales, and the customer base is concentrated: BP Berau, PT Kideco Jaya Agung and PT Freeport Indonesia each accounted for more than a tenth of consolidated revenue in FY2025 [S4].

The strategy is to convert the order book into long-life contracts and to diversify the customer and commodity mix. At the end of FY2025 the company disclosed US$4,439.0m of unsatisfied performance obligations, dominated by Mining, and the note states that management expects US$1,134.7m to be recognised as revenue in 2026 [S4]. In July 2026 it added two coal-mining services agreements in Kapuas, Central Kalimantan — one with PT Pesona Bara Cakrawala worth US$431.2m over the life of mine, and one with PT Cakrawala Bara Persada worth US$89.6m — and it completed a US$65.8m subscription for 19.9% of PT Singaraja Putra Tbk (SINI) [S3]. The non-coal thrust is visible in the same record: the INPEX Masela OLNG perimeter contract of Rp989.0bn running to March 2029, the Reko Diq earthworks contract of US$17.5m, and the HBS group's gold-services contracts with Harmony Gold, Newmont and St Barbara [S3][S2]. The HBS group itself was acquired at an estimated US$25.8m in 2025 [S3]. Those awards sit outside the FY2025 order book and are only partly quantified: the base case credits the disclosed contract values of PBC, CBP, INPEX and Reko Diq over their terms as the FY2027 revenue step, while the HBS acquired entities' revenue contribution is not separately disclosed and is not sized in the base; the HBS gold/copper contracts are a bull-case driver, not a base-case input [S3][S2]. The Petrindo-group captive mine pipeline named in the annual report — Tamtama Perkasa, Global Bara Mandiri, Multi Tambangjaya Utama and Daya Bumindo Karunia — is excluded from both because no contract values are disclosed, even though the group entities already appear among the related-party receivables [S2][S3]. The SINI relationship is both a customer and a shareholder link: SINI bought Petrosea's KMS coal mine in June 2026, and the new contracts are with SINI-affiliated entities [S3].

The controlling shareholder is PT Kreasi Jasa Persada (KJP), which held 45.3% at the end of February 2026; PT Caraka Reksa Optima held 24.4% and the public 30.1% [S2]. KJP is a subsidiary of PT Petrindo Jaya Kreasi Tbk (CUAN), and the ultimate beneficial owner is Prajogo Pangestu [S2]. The group structure matters for the investment case: Petrosea is the listed contractor inside the Barito ecosystem, and the SINI transaction is an intra-group asset sale and cross-holding rather than an arm's-length third-party deal [S3].

Indonesian mining services is a scale business. Contractors compete on fleet availability, utilisation, safety record, stripping cost per BCM and the ability to finance equipment against multi-year contracts. Petrosea sits in the large-contract tier alongside the other listed contractors, and its competitive position rests on the owned fleet, the Barito-group customer access and a long operating record in coal and mineral projects [S2]. The industry's demand driver is not the spot coal price directly but the stripping and development budgets of coal and mineral miners; when coal prices fall, clients defer overburden and new awards, and when prices rise the reverse happens with a lag [S4][S7].

The house coal deck has Newcastle at 118.0 for FY2027E against a spot of 150.3, so the deck itself assumes a lower forward price than today's spot. For a contractor that is a demand signal: a lower forward price slows client capex and contract awards, which is why our revenue growth moderates after FY2026E even though the order book is large [S4]. The oil deck's Brent path matters more directly through diesel and equipment rental, which sit in the direct-cost lines; we model a narrow cost link and partial pass-through rather than a full commodity pass-through [S4].

Regulation is the main external swing factor. From 1 January 2027 strategic-resource exports, including coal, must go through the state exporter PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia (PT DSI) under Permendag No. 15/2026 and PP No. 24/2026; the existing Eksportir Terdaftar coal licences expire at the end of 2026, and industry participants have warned that export administration could be disrupted at the changeover [S7]. Petrosea's own revenue is mostly domestic service revenue, so the direct effect is limited, but the rule affects its coal-miner clients' export logistics and therefore their capex and contract timing [S7]. The wider market regime is also hostile to concentrated-ownership names: the exchange has removed high-shareholding-concentration stocks from the IHSG calculation, MSCI opened a consultation on moving Indonesia to Standalone status, and the IHSG fell sharply on the announcement [S8][S9]. That regime is a valuation variable for this name, not an operating one.

Contract tenors are long. The new Kapuas agreements run for the life of the mine, and the legacy Vale, Kideco and Barasentosa contracts run to dates between 2028 and 2034, so the competitive battle is fought at award rather than annually [S2][S3]. Petrosea does not disclose a share of the listed contractor pool, but it positions itself as a large-contract specialist with an owned fleet and a safety and operating record long enough to qualify for the largest Indonesian mining and EPCI tenders; that is a real but narrow advantage, because the same clients can re-tender or split work between contractors at each contract renewal [S2][S4].

The moat is moderate at best. Long-life contracts, switching costs and fleet scale protect the incumbent on existing mines, but the business is cyclical, capital-intensive and exposed to customer concentration; the five forces are unfavourable on buyer power (a handful of miners), favourable on incumbency (contract continuity), and neutral-to-unfavourable on new entrants (capital and safety qualifications are barriers, but so is the ability of clients to insource or re-tender). The company's returns reflect that: group ROE has been in the single digits through the cycle [S4].

FY2025 revenue was US$886.5m, up from US$690.8m in FY2024, and gross profit was US$112.2m against US$90.3m [S4]. That consolidated figure included US$52.0m of at-a-point-in-time coal sales from the KMS mine divested on 30 June 2026; the revenue recognised over time, which is the continuing services base the forecast carries, was US$834.4m [S4]. Management's own expectation, stated in the performance-obligation note, is that US$1,134.7m will be recognised as revenue in 2026 [S4]. That level is 28.0% above the consolidated audited base of US$886.5m, but a materially faster step on the US$834.4m continuing base, because the forecast has no coal-sales line: the ratio of the US$1,134.7m expectation to the US$834.4m continuing base is the correct like-for-like growth rate, and the percentage we model is the rate on the consolidated base [S3][S4]. The gross margin fell to 12.7% from 13.1% as the revenue mix shifted toward lower-margin EPC and new mining contracts; H1 2026 then printed gross profit of US$47.0m on revenue of US$544.0m, showing that the mobilisation margin pressure is real and not a one-year anomaly [S3][S4]. The cost base is dominated by equipment operations, subcontractors and labour, with depreciation of US$90.6m and amortisation of US$14.6m in FY2025; the data pack's D&A of a small fraction of that is a direct-method cash-flow artefact, and we restate it from the notes [S4]. The restated D&A is depreciation plus amortisation, and the EBIT line is gross profit less SG&A and the final tax of US$9.7m that the LK reports inside operating costs, so FY2025A EBITDA of US$162.9m is after final tax (before it, add the final tax back) and FY2024A restates to US$96.5m on the same definition; the pack's trailing figure is lower because it carries a fraction of the charge [S4]. FY2022A and FY2023A keep the pack's D&A because the archived notes cover only the latest two years; they sit outside the valuation window.

The FY2025 balance sheet is the constraint. Capex of US$434.3m against operating cash flow of US$48.2m produced negative free cash flow, and debt rose to US$849.6m against cash of US$72.0m [S4]. At the 30 June 2026 interim cash was US$80.4m and the debt stack remained large, with the KMS receivable and the matching time-loan facility on the balance sheet; H1 2026 capex was US$43.1m of PP&E plus US$4.0m of intangibles, the 8.7% run-rate we hold for the full year [S3]. The senior term loans run to 2032-33 and carry a debt-to-equity ceiling of 3.0x, amended on 27 March 2026 from the original, tighter level, and an EBITDA-to-debt-and-interest floor of 115%, tested quarterly, while an ANZ facility for HBS needed a covenant waiver for the June 2026 compliance period [S3]. The company paid dividends of US$9.9m in FY2025 and US$3.1m in FY2024, a payout of roughly a third of parent net profit, but the enlarged debt and capex programme mean the dividend is not the anchor it is for the coal producers [S4].

Our forecast follows management's 2026 revenue expectation and the awarded contracts, not the pack's history. Revenue grows 28.0% in FY2026E to US$1,134.7m, the level management states for 2026 in the same note [S4]. We hold 8.0% for FY2027E — the annualised contribution of the post-balance-sheet awards (PBC, CBP, INPEX and Reko Diq) layered on that base — then 7.0%, 5.0% and 4.0% as the multi-year RPO converts. The path is not below the RPO conversion pace: management's 2026 expectation absorbs US$1,134.7m of the US$4,439.0m end-2025 book, the two July contracts worth US$431.2m and US$89.6m sit outside that book, and no volume decline or lost contract is assumed; the undisclosed Petrindo-group pipeline and the HBS gold/copper contracts are excluded as upside because no contract values are disclosed [S2][S3][S4]. The house coal deck's lower forward Newcastle path is a second-order demand signal for a contractor, not the revenue driver. Gross margin recovers from 9.7% to 12.7% — the FY2025 actual, not a haircut below it — as the new life-of-mine contracts mature. The engine reproduces FY2025A at an EBITDA margin of 18.4% on the restated D&A, and its FY2026E margin is 16.5%, the step down being the mobilisation gross-margin cut part offset by scale in overheads; SG&A plus final tax is held at 4.5%; capex is held at the H1 run-rate of 8.7% of revenue in FY2026E and lifts to 11.0% long run, in line with D&A, as the new contracts mobilise and the fleet is renewed [S3][S4]. Capex is the largest single swing in the valuation: it is a dollar-for-dollar deduction from each year's free cash flow, so a point of capex-to-revenue is worth the present value of that share of the explicit-period revenue stream, and the assumptions record that present value against the DCF equity value. EBITDA rises from US$186.8m to US$271.3m, but interest expense of US$68.0m keeps pre-tax profit negative in FY2026E; parent net profit is US$-14.3m in FY2026E, marginally positive at US$3.2m in FY2027E and materially positive in FY2028E [S3][S4].

**Earnings-quality flags.** The cash test is clean, not dirty: operating cash flow exceeded net profit in each of FY2023 (US$107.8m against US$12.2m), FY2024 (US$27.9m against US$9.7m) and FY2025 (US$48.2m against US$28.8m), so the accruals ratio — net profit less operating cash flow over average total assets — is negative in all three years and the profit is cash-backed; the reader can reproduce it from those figures and total assets of US$728.0m, US$867.3m and US$1,582.9m [S2][S4]. Cash conversion narrowed each year as the fleet build absorbed working capital but stayed above one. The real flag is the one-off: FY2025 other gains of US$34.5m were almost the whole pre-tax profit of US$39.3m, so recurring earnings were a small fraction of the reported US$28.8m parent profit; we set other non-operating income to zero from FY2026E [S4]. The related-party channel is material and we read it as optics-class, not manipulation-class. Related-party revenue was US$109.6m, or 12.4% of consolidated revenue, in FY2025, and US$96.5m, or 17.8% of consolidated revenue, in H1 2026 [S4][S3]. At 30 June 2026 related-party trade receivables were US$103.5m (from US$69.8m at December 2025) plus US$89.9m of other current related-party receivables, the KMS current portion; the trade receivables alone were 6.8% of consolidated assets, and against H1 revenue of US$544.0m and total equity of US$321.3m they are a large share of both [S4][S3]. The largest trade-receivable debtor is PT Cristian Eka Pratama, followed by PT Daya Bumindo Karunia, PT Multi Tambangjaya Utama, PT Pasir Bara Prima, Fluor Petrosea Joint Operation and PT Borneo Bangun Banua — several of them Petrindo-group entities — so the receivable book is itself a group exposure [S3]. The KMS sale was disclosed at a US$5.8m loss on divestment, so it did not flatter earnings, and the current receivable was collected in July 2026; the trade receivables remain at the valuation date [S3]. We classify both the SINI/KMS transaction and the receivable as optics-class: disclosed in the interim notes, priced and reported, with no confirmed manipulation finding. The company is not on the exchange's special-monitoring board and carries no special notation in the record we hold [S0].

The method set is the MINING_CONTRACTORS house set: a free-cash-flow-to-firm DCF as the primary method, with EV/EBITDA and EV/Sales as cross-checks. A contractor is valued on the cash its contract book generates after the capex needed to execute it, not on a coal reserve or a spot selling price, so DCF-FCFF is the right primary. The cross-checks matter because the equity is thin relative to debt: EV/EBITDA captures the operating value that the DCF might discount too harshly during a capex-heavy phase, and EV/Sales captures the contracted revenue scale. We drop the industry's usual P/E cross-check because the trailing metric is unusable here: FY2025A parent net profit of US$28.8m includes a US$34.5m non-recurring other gain, so the trailing P/E would capitalise a one-off-inflated peak [S4]. The P/E weight is carried by EV/Sales instead.

The cost of capital is built from a risk-free rate of 4.9%, a mature-market ERP of 4.2% and an Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%, with an unlevered beta of 1.00 from the industry default and a levered beta of 1.50 at the company's debt-to-equity ratio [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 15.0% and a WACC of 11.2%. The debt leg of the WACC is the USD risk-free rate plus the house macro deck's pre-tax corporate spread, a seed deck input, giving a pre-tax cost of debt of 6.9% [S12]; it is the discount-rate input, not the interest cost in the P&L. The P&L uses the 8.0% opening-debt cost in our assumptions, which is closer to the FY2025 actual interest expense than the deck's discount rate [S4]. We disclose the difference rather than override the deck: at the 39.2% debt weight and the 22.0% tax rate, moving to the P&L rate changes the WACC by the after-tax debt weight times the difference, and the WACC columns in the sensitivity table bracket it [S12]. The WACC is high because the balance sheet is levered and the equity beta is high; it is not a cautious add-on, it is the arithmetic of the capital structure [S4].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of US$990.8m and an equity value of Rp532 per share, with the terminal value contributing 45.0% of the total. The explicit-period cash flows are weak in FY2026E because working capital absorbs the EBITDA, then improve as the new contracts mobilise and the fleet build is complete; long-run capex is set at the D&A ratio so the terminal value does not assume a fleet that is run down [S3][S4]. The net-debt bridge uses the 30 June 2026 balance sheet and measures cash as cash and cash equivalents of US$80.4m plus other financial assets of US$11.1m, so the bridge is marginally less levered than on the LK's cash line alone — a gap inside our tolerance that does not change the valuation; it adds the SINI stake at cost and the non-current KMS receivable, but not the current KMS receivable because the matching Time Loan is already in net debt [S3].

The cross-checks diverge, and the divergence is the point. EV/EBITDA at 9.7x is applied to the engine's trailing FY2025A EBITDA of US$162.9m — not to FY2026E; the trailing figure includes the US$52.0m KMS coal-sales contribution that the forecast does not carry — and gives Rp1,581 per share, about 197.1% above the DCF, because the multiple capitalises pre-capex, pre-interest EBITDA while the DCF deducts capex and interest; for a contractor carrying this debt stack that gap is expected. EV/Sales at 1.5x on FY2025A revenue of US$886.5m gives Rp1,134, about 113.2% above the DCF on the same trailing basis; it is not distorted by the one-off gain, but it also ignores capex and interest [S0][S4]. The peer table shows why the cross-checks are capped at their house weights: the MINING_CONTRACTORS basket is the exchange's contractor classification, and its EV/EBITDA contributors span the small-cap and offshore-service tail, with only the subset carrying positive trailing EBITDA supplying a usable multiple. The contributing multiples range from the low single digits to a high double-digit outlier, so the median — not the mean — is the anchor, and the spread is why the method is a cross-check rather than a target: at a high-end peer multiple the value would sit far above the DCF, at a low-end one far below it. The high end includes names such as DEWA and PKPK, whose multiples reflect contracted utility or small-cap cash flows rather than contractor risk; the peer table lists each contributor, so the cross-check value of Rp1,581 can be re-scaled to any of them. We keep the broad basket rather than narrow to a handful of coal names, because a very small sample is less stable than the broad median; the DCF carries 60.0% for that reason, and the EV/EBITDA cross-check carries 25.0%. Both cross-checks use FY2025A metrics, and we disclose that rather than relabel them as forward multiples.

With weights of DCF 60.0%, EV/EBITDA 25.0% and EV/Sales 15.0%, the weighted methods give a base-case fundamental value today of Rp885; probability-weighting the three business scenarios' twelve-month values gives the twelve-month fundamental value of Rp1,235, below the market price [S0].

The table shows the DCF against WACC and terminal growth and the twelve-month value against revenue growth and gross margin. Capex is not a separate axis, but it is the largest single sensitivity: it is a dollar-for-dollar deduction from free cash flow, so a point of capex-to-revenue changes the explicit-period value by the present value of that share of the revenue stream, before any change in terminal capex, and the assumptions record that present value against the DCF equity value [S4]. The margin and growth axes bracket the business scenarios below.

The konglo lens then does the regime step. At Rp2,320 the shares trade at 2.2x the probability-weighted fundamental value today of Rp1,077.5 (0.77 in log terms) [S0][S11]. The same price is a smaller multiple of the twelve-month fundamental value of Rp1,235 — the ratio of the price to that value is correspondingly below the 2.2x shown — and the engine's lens, set by the house konglo deck, applies its closure to that gap: with no regime flags the base regime closes 30.0% of the log gap and gives Rp2,113, the bear regime closes 70.0% and gives Rp1,555, and the bull regime lets the premium re-expand and gives Rp2,984 [S10][S11]. The probability-weighted target across the three regimes — the deck's 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull weights — is Rp2,191. That target is not the base-regime output — which is Rp2,113 — and it is not a fundamental re-rating; it is the deterministic probability-weighted most-likely price for a name whose premium is a regime variable [S10][S11].

The premium is not a constrained-float squeeze: the registry free float is 27.6%, above the regulatory minimum, with no HSC listing, no index deletion and no enforcement on record [S0][S11]. It is a group-flow premium. KJP holds 45.3% and CARA 24.4% [S2]; the group has an active capital-markets agenda in the SINI rights issue and KMS asset sale, the two SINI-linked life-of-mine contracts, and the 1.7% rights issue due for approval at the 23 November 2026 EGM [S3][S5]; and the two controlling blocks hold most of the register, so the disclosed float overstates the actively traded supply even though it satisfies the rule [S2][S11]. The base regime's 30.0% closure is tied to the dated catalysts inside the twelve-month window: the 23 November EGM, the 30 April 2027 MSCI feedback deadline and the 30 June 2027 classification decision. A Standalone decision or a failed rights issue would move the name toward the bear regime [S8][S9][S10]. The reverse DCF says the price requires FY2027E revenue growth of about 21.4% against our 8.0%; the konglo lens is the only reason the target is not closer to the fundamental value [S0][S4].

The downside risks are leverage, refinancing, margin, regulation and the regime. Leverage: net debt is high relative to EBITDA, and interest expense of US$68.0m against EBIT of US$50.6m keeps pre-tax profit negative, so a modest margin miss deepens the loss; the company has already shown a small H1 2026 continuing-operations profit only with the help of non-recurring other gains [S3][S4]. Refinancing and covenants: at 30 June 2026 the long-term loans fall due as US$56.5m within a year, US$322.4m between one and five years and US$199.3m beyond five years, alongside US$109.3m of bonds; the senior term loans carry a debt-to-equity ceiling of 3.0x, amended on 27 March 2026 from the original, tighter level, and an EBITDA-to-debt-and-interest floor of 115%, tested quarterly, the bonds add an EBITDA-to-interest-and-instalments floor of 1.15x, and an ANZ facility for HBS needed a waiver for the June 2026 compliance period [S3]. A higher reset cost on the debt stack, or a tightening of those covenants, is the fastest way for the equity value to fall below our bear case; the bear scenario raises the cost of debt by the same shock the bull lowers it, so the refinancing stress is in the scenario set and not only in this paragraph [S3]. Margin: the new EPC and mining contracts are mobilising at lower margins than the legacy book, and the H1 2026 gross profit of US$47.0m on revenue of US$544.0m is the evidence; a failure to recover toward the FY2025 level would leave the equity value below our base [S3][S4]. Regulation: the PT DSI export channel from 1 January 2027 could disrupt coal-miner clients' exports and delay contract awards; the direct revenue effect on Petrosea is small, but the timing effect on coal capex is not [S7]. Regime: MSCI's Standalone consultation, the HSC/IHSG exclusion and the free-float roadmap are dated catalysts that can compress the konglo premium faster than our lens assumes [S8][S9]. Governance and counterparty: the SINI/KMS related-party transaction and the 19.9% cross-holding are disclosed but concentrated; related-party revenue was 17.8% of H1 2026 revenue, and at 30 June 2026 related-party trade receivables were US$103.5m with other current related-party receivables of US$89.9m — the KMS portion was collected in July, but the trade receivables remain at the valuation date — so a collection delay or a group counterparty strain is a real cash risk, not a footnote [S3]. The bear scenario adds a working-capital drag from slower related-party collection on top of the revenue and margin cuts [S0].

The business scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers: revenue growth and gross margin plus the cost of debt and working capital. The bear case cuts revenue growth and gross margin, resets the debt cost higher and adds a related-party collection drag, and values the equity at Rp650; the bull case mirrors all four and values it at Rp2,257; the base is Rp1,017, with probabilities of 25.0%, 50.0% and 25.0% [S0]. The bear value therefore already contains the refinancing and receivable-collection stress, not just a revenue miss. The konglo regime scenarios are separate and are set by the house konglo deck: the base regime closes 30.0% of the log gap and gives Rp2,113, the bear closes 70.0% and gives Rp1,555, and the bull lets the premium re-expand and gives Rp2,984 [S10][S11]. The probability-weighted target, on the deck's 25.0%/50.0%/25.0% regime weights, is Rp2,191; the gap between the fundamental value and the target is the regime premium, and the gap between the target and the price is our expected return [S0].

Signposts that would change the view: a faster-than-expected ramp of the SINI-linked contracts, the INPEX award or Reko Diq would lift the base-case revenue and margin path; approval and completion of the proposed rights issue would fund working capital but would not repair the balance sheet — at 170m new shares it is 1.7% of paid-up capital and dilutes non-participants by at most 1.7%, and the maximum gross proceeds are the value of those shares at the current price, a small fraction of the US$849.6m debt stack [S5]; a decision by MSCI to keep Indonesia in Emerging Markets, or a clear free-float fix, would slow the premium compression and support the target; conversely, an adverse MSCI decision, a covenant tightening or a new related-party receivable would compress the lens and the fundamental value together [S3][S7][S9][S10].

Petrosea is a konglo name in the registry we run: the controller is Prajogo Pangestu through KJP and CUAN, the group role is the listed mining contractor and EPC arm, and the company holds 19.9% of SINI after the July 2026 rights issue [S2][S3]. Ownership is concentrated — KJP 45.3%, CARA 24.4% and the public 30.1% at the end of February 2026 — and the registry free float is 27.6%, above the regulatory minimum and compliant [S0][S2][S11]. The premium is therefore not a rule-driven squeeze: the name is not on the exchange's HSC list, has no index deletion and no OJK enforcement in the record, and the lens applies its default compression with no regime adjustment [S11][S10]. What sustains the premium is group flow — the controller's capital-markets agenda and the two controlling blocks holding most of the register — not a float shortage recognised by the index rules [S11][S2].

The related-party channel is the main governance fact. SINI bought KMS from Petrosea for a transaction value of US$97.0m, booked at a US$5.8m loss on divestment, paid partly through a current receivable that was received in July 2026 and a non-current receivable of US$12.4m due in 2027, and Petrosea then subscribed US$65.8m to the SINI rights issue for a 19.9% stake [S3]. Related-party revenue was US$109.6m, or 12.4% of consolidated revenue, in FY2025 and US$96.5m, or 17.8% of consolidated revenue, in H1 2026; at 30 June 2026 related-party trade receivables were US$103.5m plus US$89.9m of other current related-party receivables, with the largest trade debtors being PT Cristian Eka Pratama and Petrindo-group entities such as PT Daya Bumindo Karunia, PT Multi Tambangjaya Utama and PT Borneo Bangun Banua [S4][S3]. The two new life-of-mine coal contracts signed on the same day are with SINI-affiliated entities and are worth US$431.2m and US$89.6m [S3]. We treat the transaction as disclosed and optics-class, not manipulation-class — the sale was at a small loss, the current receivable was collected in July, and the stake is at cost in our bridge — but the concentration of revenue, receivables and equity value in one group counterparty is a structural governance discount that the lens captures through the regime scenarios [S3][S10].

On dividends, the company paid US$9.9m in FY2025 and US$3.1m in FY2024, a payout of roughly a third of parent net profit, but the enlarged debt and capex programme mean the dividend is not the anchor it is for the coal producers; the rights issue proposed for November 2026 would fund working capital and dilute non-participating holders by at most 1.7%, but at 1.7% of paid-up capital it is working-capital funding, not a balance-sheet repair [S4][S5]. The auditor's opinion is unmodified in the record we hold, and no pledged-share, auditor down-tier or special-notation flag appears in the archived filings [S0][S4]. ESG exposures are the standard contractor set: safety and mine-site rehabilitation, emissions from the diesel fleet, and community relations in Kalimantan; the annual report discloses the sustainability framework but no quantified emissions-reduction target that would change the valuation [S2].

The dated catalysts are the 23 November 2026 extraordinary shareholders' meeting on the proposed rights issue, the 30 April 2027 MSCI consultation feedback deadline and the 30 June 2027 MSCI classification decision [S5][S9]. The non-current KMS receivable of US$12.4m falls due in 2027, the INPEX OLNG contract runs to 1 March 2029 and the Reko Diq earthworks targeted completion in July 2026 [S3]. The company's quarterly interim accounts and the FY2026 audited results are the operating checkpoints; we will compare overburden volume, coal production and the gross margin on the new contracts against the base case [S2][S3].

The KPIs we watch between updates are: overburden removal volume and coal production from the mining services book (FY2025: 135.2 million BCM and 19.2 million tonnes) [S2]; revenue conversion against the US$4,439.0m order book [S4]; gross margin, which printed US$47.0m of gross profit on US$544.0m of revenue in H1 2026 [S3]; net debt, interest cover, the loan maturity ladder (US$56.5m within a year, US$322.4m between one and five years, US$199.3m beyond) and the bonds (US$109.3m), and the covenant tests; the related-party receivables and the 19.9% stake's mark; the INPEX and gold-services contribution; and the free-float/HSC/MSCI regime signals [S8][S9][S11]. A sustained recovery in gross margin above 10.7% with positive free cash flow would be the first evidence that the base case is too cautious; a further related-party receivable or a delay in the new contracts would be the first evidence that it is too optimistic.

Petrosea was founded more than half a century ago and has operated through several commodity cycles;
Indonesian mining contractors typically earn thin margins on large asset bases, and the market has
historically valued the large, liquid names at a premium to book while smaller contractors trade
closer to replacement cost. The Barito group's recent capital-markets activity has changed the
shareholder base and the liquidity profile of several of its listed vehicles, which is why the
regime lens matters alongside the operating model.

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is management's own revenue expectation, stated verbatim in Note 30 as US$1,135m of revenue to be recognised in 2026 (S4 p.118; F66); the +28.0% consolidated and +36.0% continuing-base growth rates are our derivations, not a management-stated percentage. The continuing base excludes the US$52.0m of divested KMS coal sales (S4 p.117; F38/F39). FY2027E 8% is the annualised contribution of the post-balance-sheet awards (PBC US$431.2m and CBP US$89.6m over life of mine, INPEX Rp989bn to 2029, Reko Diq US$17.5m) on top of that base; FY2028-30 moderate to 7/5/4% as the multi-year RPO converts. The path is not below the RPO conversion pace; management's 2026 expectation absorbs US$1,135m of the US$4,438.952m end-2025 book, so the remaining book supports the mid-single-digit path without a lost contract or a volume decline. The house coal deck's lower forward Newcastle path is a second-order demand signal for a contractor, not the revenue driver. The undisclosed Petrindo-group pipeline (S2 p.20) and the HBS gold/copper contracts are excluded because no contract values are disclosed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: H1 2026 gross margin was 8.65% as new EPC and mining contracts mobilised at lower initial margins; we hold 9.7% for FY2026E (H2 fleet utilisation improves) and recover to the FY2025 actual 12.66% by 2030 as the new SINI-linked life-of-mine contracts mature. The long-run rate is the last actual, not a haircut below it; the mix effect is sourced from the half-year result.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Fuel and equipment rental sit inside operations of plant and equipment and rental of heavy equipment (US$194m and US$61m in FY2025 direct costs); we treat 5% of COGS as Brent-linked, a deliberately narrow share because most direct cost is subcontractors, labour and materials.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Half of the Brent-linked fuel/rental cost is assumed recovered through contract fuel-escalation clauses; mining-service contracts are quoted on indexed rates, but no disclosed clause quantifies the pass-through, so 50% is the analyst's central case.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: SG&A plus final tax: FY2025 selling/admin was 5.05% of revenue and final tax 1.10%, but H1 2026 selling/admin ran at 3.7% of revenue as scale rose; 4.5% is the central full-year rate, not the FY2025 fixed-cost ratio.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated LK total D&A (depreciation 90.552 plus amortisation 14.605) was 11.86% of FY2025 revenue; H1 2026 D&A annualises at a similar rate as the enlarged fleet is depreciated. Held at 12.0% and eased to 11.0% as capex normalises.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was 49% of revenue in a fleet-expansion year; H1 2026 capex was US$47.1m (PP&E US$43.087m plus intangibles US$4.050m), 8.7% of H1 revenue, as the build completed and contracts mobilised. We hold the H1 run-rate at 8.7% for FY2026E (no sourced H2 step-up exists), then lift capex to 11% long run - in line with the 11% D&A ratio - so the enlarged fleet is maintained in real terms rather than run down. Sensitivity arithmetic — at FY2026E revenue, 1pp of capex/revenue is US$11.3m of annual FCF; across the ten explicit years its present value is about US$92.5m, roughly 31% of the US$296.2m DCF equity value, so the capex path is the largest single swing in the valuation. The engine's sensitivity grid has no capex axis, so this arithmetic is disclosed here and the report's DCF table lets the reader trace it.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was 12.6% of revenue; the H1 2026 ratio is distorted by the KMS related-party receivable, which converts to the SINI stake and cash in July 2026, so the normalised FY2025 ratio is held.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 income tax was 10.9% of PBT after the final tax already charged above EBIT; 12% keeps the LK's effective rate and allows for the non-deductible items shown in the tax note.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest expense of US$55.7m on average debt of US$623.6m is 8.9%; the disclosed IDR facilities price at IndONIA plus a margin and the bonds/sukuk carry fixed coupons (6.50%-9.50%), so 8.0% is the forward blended P&L cost. This is deliberately separate from the WACC debt leg, which the engine takes from the house macro deck as the USD risk-free rate plus the deck's 200bp corporate spread (6.93%, S12); the report discloses both rates and the WACC sensitivity table brackets the difference.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income of US$2.7m on opening cash of US$114.9m is 2.35%; 2.0% allows for the restricted balances that earn less.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new net borrowing assumed: the KMS proceeds repay the Time Loan 2 and H1 2026 operating cash flow turns positive, so debt is held flat in the base case.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring other income assumed; FY2025's US$34.5m other gain is non-recurring (acquisition-related) and is not capitalised.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 minorities took 17.7% of net profit after the PTHDK/PTHDS acquisitions; H1 2026 minorities were negative during mobilisation. 10% is a smoothed central case between the FY2024 2.5% and FY2025 17.7%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2024 and FY2025 dividends paid were 32% and 34% of parent net profit; the company has no fixed policy and the group has heavy capex and debt, so 35% is the central payout rather than the engine's 100% default.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No share change in the base case: the 170m-share rights issue is not final and still needs the 23 November 2026 EGM approval, so it is treated as a catalyst, not a base-case dilution.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.0% terminal growth for a USD-reporting contractor with life-of-mine contracts; below Indonesian nominal GDP and consistent with the house terminal-growth default, so no terminal value is created by an unsourced growth premium.

challenges.challenge: The FY2026E revenue growth of 28% — the model's first key input and the base off which every later year compounds — is justified as "management's own revenue expectation for 2026, which is 28% above the FY2025 actual" [S4][S3]. No archived source states it. S2's "Prospek Usaha & Target 2026" (pp.158-159) is qualitative: the company "projects continued revenue growth through a combination of organic expansion and the acquisition of new strategic contracts" and "targets net profit growth in 2026"; it gives no revenue percentage or amount. S3's only targets are contract values and a bond-raising target; S4 is the audited financial statements. The only 28% in the record is the historical FY2025 revenue growth of 28.32% (S2 p.17: 886.46 vs 690.81), which appears to have been carried forward and relabelled as management guidance. The level itself is not obviously wrong (H1 2026 continuing revenue was +59.6% yoy), but the stated basis is false and the source list cannot support it.
challenges.answer: The premise that no archived source states the expectation is not correct: S4 Note 30 p.118 (also S2 p.379) reads verbatim 'Management expects that US$ 1 ,135 million will be recognized as revenue for the year 2026'. We added F66 quoting it, reworded the report to cite management's disclosed dollar amount rather than asserting a management-stated percentage, and made clear that the 28% is our derived growth rate on the consolidated base (management gives the level, not the rate). The level is unchanged. The only 28% in the record is indeed the historical FY2025 growth; the base is now sourced to the disclosed level and to RPO conversion, not to that history.

challenges.challenge: The FY2025A revenue of US$886.459m is the consolidated figure and includes US$52.016m of at-a-point-in-time coal sales from the KMS mine that was sold on 30 June 2026; the overtime subtotal is US$834.443m (S4 Note 30, p.117). FY2026E revenue of US$1,134.7m is a continuing-operations forecast with no coal-sales line (S3 Note 30: Mining 300.435, Construction 196.564, EPCI 28.216, Services 17.824, Others 0.944). Applying +28% to the consolidated base therefore overstates like-for-like growth: against US$834.443m the same forecast is +36.0%. The report calls the coal line "small" but it is 5.9% of revenue and sits in a divested subsidiary.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now shows the explicit bridge: FY2025A consolidated US$886.459m = US$834.443m recognised over time + US$52.016m at-a-point-in-time KMS coal sales, and states that the 28% modelled rate is on the consolidated audited base while the ratio of the US$1,135m expectation to the US$834.443m continuing base is the correct like-for-like rate. The consolidated base is retained because the model's FY2025 history must tie to the audited LK and management's 2026 expectation is a consolidated figure; the forecast has no coal-sales line, so the divested revenue is not carried forward. The continuing-base growth rate is stated in the assumptions basis and reproducible from the two report placeholders.

challenges.challenge: §4 explains the EV/EBITDA cross-check as "the multiple capitalises FY2026E EBITDA before the capex and interest that the DCF deducts". The engine applies 9.666x to FY2025A EBITDA of US$142.06m (fund record methods.ev_ebitda.metric), not FY2026E US$184.48m; the value is Rp1,219. The multiple is the median of only eight observations spanning 2.0x-48.1x (PKPK 48.1x, ATLA 26.9x, DEWA 12.9x, UNIQ 10.5x, WINS 8.8x, RUIS 6.3x, SUNI 5.5x, MYOH 2.0x) drawn from an 18-name basket that is not a pure contractor set. The stated reason for the 93.9% divergence is wrong, and the cross-check's sensitivity to the peer set is not shown.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now attributes the EV/EBITDA cross-check to the engine's trailing FY2025A EBITDA (not FY2026E), discloses that it carries the divested coal-sales EBITDA, and explains the peer set: the basket is the exchange's contractor classification, only the subset with positive trailing EBITDA yields a multiple, the contributors range from the low single digits to a high double-digit outlier, and the median is the anchor while DEWA/PKPK represent the high end (contracted utility/small-cap cash flows). The peer table lists every contributor, so the cross-check value can be re-scaled linearly to the interquartile or DEWA-level multiple; the weight stays at 25% for that reason.

challenges.challenge: The P/E cross-check applies 10.256x to FY2025A parent net profit of US$28.808m (fund record methods.pe.metric) — a year that includes a US$34.545m non-recurring "other gains and losses" credit (S4 p.14; PBT US$39.278m, tax US$4.272m, NP US$35.006m). The model itself treats that gain as non-recurring and sets other_nonop to zero from FY2026E. §4 says the P/E value is low "because FY2026E earnings are depressed by interest and the multiple is applied to a trough year"; in fact it capitalises a one-off-inflated peak year. Recurring FY2025 parent earnings are only ~US$3-5m, so a P/E on recurring earnings would be far higher or meaningless.
challenges.answer: The P/E cross-check is dropped, its 15% weight is reassigned to EV/Sales, and section 4 explains that FY2025A parent net profit of US$28.808m carries a US$34.545m non-recurring other gain, so the trailing P/E would capitalise a one-off-inflated peak and a P/E on recurring earnings would be meaningless. The 'trough year' explanation is removed, and section 4 now discloses that both retained cross-checks use FY2025A metrics rather than relabelling them as forward multiples.

challenges.challenge: §4 says "At Rp2,320 the shares trade at 2.5x the twelve-month fundamental value of Rp1,054 (0.93 in log terms)" and that "the lens keeps 30.0% of that log premium in the base regime and gives a target of Rp2,121". The engine divides price by today's probability-weighted fundamental value of Rp918.37 (2,320/918.37 = 2.526, ln = 0.9267) and applies (2.526)^(1-c) to the 12-month value of Rp1,054.19; 2,320/1,054.19 is 2.20x (ln 0.79). The 30% base regime gives Rp2,016.74, not Rp2,121; Rp2,121 is the probability-weighted average of the three regime targets (25% x 1,392.07 + 50% x 2,016.74 + 25% x 3,060). The printed numbers cannot reproduce the lens, and §4 mislabels the base-regime output. §5 states the scenarios correctly.
challenges.answer: The model was re-run with the round-1 fixes, so the lens numbers now print 2.35x the probability-weighted fundamental value today of Rp987.1 (log 0.85), a twelve-month fundamental value of Rp1,131.4, base-regime Rp2,057.7, bear Rp1,462.0, bull Rp3,022.6 and probability-weighted target Rp2,150.0. Section 4 now shows both denominators, says the price is a smaller multiple of the twelve-month value, and states that Rp2,150 is the probability-weighted target, not the base-regime output (which is printed as Rp2,058). The stale qc_justification was updated to the current lens.

challenges.challenge: The bear business case (25% probability, Rp442) shocks only revenue growth (-6pp) and gross margin (-2.5pp). It contains no refinancing, covenant or debt-cost shock, although FY2026E net debt/EBITDA is 4.5x (US$829.4m/US$184.5m), EBIT covers interest only 0.71x (US$48.3m/US$68.0m), the 30 June debt stack is US$831.6m, and the model assumes an 8.0% cost of debt while the FY2025 actual was 8.9% (US$55.699m on average debt US$623.6m). A 100bp reset on US$831.6m adds ~US$8.3m pre-tax, about a sixth of FY2026E EBIT. Leverage is listed as a prose risk but is not in the scenario set.
challenges.answer: The bear scenario already resets the cost of debt higher (the mirrored bull lowers it by the same shock) and adds a working-capital drag, and the scenario table shows the resulting equity value. Section 5 now sets out the debt maturity ladder from S3 Note 25: US$56.531m due within a year, US$322.439m in one to five years and US$199.320m beyond five years, alongside US$109.254m of bonds, with the senior term loan D/E ceiling of 2.5x and EBITDA-to-debt-and-interest floor of 115%, the bonds' 1.15x EBITDA cover and the ANZ waiver for the June 2026 period. The shocks are mirrored in absolute percentage points on the same four drivers (the industry default), so the bear is not one-sided.

challenges.section: 5. Investment risks and scenario analysis / 6. Governance
challenges.challenge: Related-party exposure is under-quantified. At 30 June 2026 related-party trade receivables were US$103.461m (up from US$69.790m at Dec-25) and other related-party receivables were US$89.934m (the KMS current portion; nil at Dec-25) — US$193.4m in total, 35.6% of H1 2026 revenue and 21.8% of FY2025 revenue. SINI-affiliated entities are the counterparty on the new US$520.8m of life-of-mine contracts and SINI bought the KMS mine. §3 flags only the US$12.4m non-current receivable; the EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS output contract requires related-party flows as a percentage of revenue and the report gives none.
challenges.answer: Related-party flows are now quantified on both periods: FY2025 revenue of US$109.558m (12.36% of consolidated revenue) and H1 2026 revenue of US$96.537m (17.75%); at 30 June 2026 trade receivables were US$103.461m (from US$69.790m) plus US$89.934m of other current related-party receivables, against H1 revenue of US$543.983m and total equity of US$321.285m. The largest trade debtors are named (PT Cristian Eka Pratama, then PT Daya Bumindo Karunia, PT Multi Tambangjaya Utama, PT Pasir Bara Prima, Fluor Petrosea JO and PT Borneo Bangun Banua). The text notes the US$89.9m KMS portion was collected on 24 July 2026 while the US$103.5m trade receivable remains at the valuation date, and the bear adds a collection/working-capital drag.

challenges.challenge: The base case decelerates revenue growth to 8/7/5/4% and 2% terminal with no sourced basis beyond "the house coal deck's lower forward Newcastle path slows client capex". Against that: FY2025 unsatisfied performance obligations of US$4,438.952m are 5.0x FY2025 revenue (5.3x the US$834.4m continuing base); the two July 2026 life-of-mine contracts worth US$520.8m are after the balance sheet and not in the RPO; and S2 p.20 describes an ongoing captive pipeline of Petrindo-group mines (Tamtama Perkasa, Global Bara Mandiri, Multi Tambangjaya Utama, Daya Bumindo Karunia). A contractor's revenue is contract-driven, not Newcastle-driven, so the coal path is at best a second-order demand signal.
challenges.answer: The growth basis is rewritten to be contract/RPO-driven, not Newcastle-driven. FY2027E 8% is the annualised contribution of the post-balance-sheet PBC and CBP contracts plus INPEX and Reko Diq; FY2028-30 7/5/4% is RPO conversion. Management's 2026 expectation of US$1,135m absorbs that amount of the US$4,438.952m end-2025 book, so the path is not below the RPO conversion pace and no volume decline or lost contract is assumed. The two July contracts (US$431.228m and US$89.605m) sit outside the end-2025 book. The unbooked Petrindo-group pipeline and the HBS gold/copper contracts are stated and excluded because no contract values are disclosed; the coal deck is framed as a second-order demand signal.

challenges.challenge: The capex path is internally inconsistent and conservatively front-loaded. FY2026E capex is 12.0% of revenue (US$136.2m), but H1 2026 actual capex was US$47.1m (PP&E US$43.087m + intangibles US$4.050m, 8.7% of H1 revenue; S3 p.14), implying H2 capex of ~US$89m — 15.1% of H2 revenue, nearly double the H1 rate — while the basis says "the build completed and contracts mobilised". Long-run capex then sits at 10% against D&A of 11% while revenue grows 4% a year, i.e. the fleet is assumed to shrink in real terms. Each 1pp of capex/revenue is worth ~US$13-16m of annual FCF.
challenges.answer: FY2026E capex is now held at the H1 2026 run-rate of 8.7% of revenue (PP&E US$43.087m plus intangibles US$4.050m), not 12%; the path then lifts to 11% long run, equal to the 11% D&A ratio, so the fleet is maintained rather than run down and terminal capex is consistent with a stable real fleet at 2% terminal growth. The assumptions record the sensitivity explicitly: at FY2026E revenue, 1pp of capex/revenue is US$11.3m of annual FCF and about US$92.5m of present value across the ten explicit years, roughly 31% of the US$296.2m DCF equity value. Sections 3 and 4 state that capex is the largest single swing and that the engine's sensitivity grid has no capex axis, so the arithmetic is disclosed in the assumptions and traceable in the DCF table.

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality paragraph is directionally wrong. It says "the accruals picture is not clean: FY2025 net profit of US$28.8m against operating cash flow of US$48.2m is flattered by non-cash gains and by the working-capital build". Net profit is below operating cash flow (NI-CFO = -US$19.3m on parent NP; accruals ratio ~-1.6% of average total assets), which is the opposite of the Sloan flag the card asks for; the working-capital build reduces OCF rather than flattering NP. The real flag is that the US$34.545m other gain is 88% of PBT, so recurring FY2025 earnings are ~US$4-5m. The paragraph also omits the accruals ratio, cash-conversion trend and related-party % required by the card's output contract.
challenges.answer: The direction is corrected: operating cash flow exceeded net profit in FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025, so the accruals ratio is negative in all three years and the profit is cash-backed; the working-capital build reduces OCF rather than flattering net profit, and cash conversion narrowed each year but stayed above one.
